The Society of Jesus, whose members are called Jesuits, is a Catholic religious order founded by the Basque soldier turned priest Ignatius of Loyola and his companions, and approved by the pope in 1540. Run with strict discipline by a Superior General in Rome, it became the spearhead of the Catholic answer to the Reformation, and Jesuit theologians spoke at the Council of Trent.

Jesuits worked on a world scale:

  • Schools. They ran hundreds of colleges in Europe and the colonies and trained much of the Catholic elite.
  • Missions. Francis Xavier went to Goa and Japan; Matteo Ricci reached Beijing; Jesuits in Vietnam helped shape the Vietnamese alphabet; António Vieira preached in Brazil. In South America they ran the reductions among the Guaraní, and they worked among peoples from Chile to the Great Lakes, among them the Yaqui of northern Mexico.
  • Knowledge. They brought cinchona bark to Europe as a remedy for malaria, and mapped, translated and watched the stars.

Their power made enemies. Portugal expelled them in 1759, France and Spain followed, and the pope suppressed the order in 1773. It was restored in 1814 and is now the largest order of men in the Catholic Church. Pope Francis, elected in 2013, was the first Jesuit pope.
